phases: The Words of the Plan B

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a short period of time in which something is possible
ready to act immediately if you are needed
a second plan you use if the first one fails
with almost no extra time or space
a problem that causes another problem somewhere else
to delay a decision so that you have longer to decide
to cancel something that was planned
to send something or somebody along a different path

paras: The room has no windows and eleven screens, and almost nobody who flies out of that airport will ever hear it mentioned. Marcus Bell has worked in it for nine years. His title is duty controller, and the shortest description of the job is that he decides what happens next when the plan stops working. On an ordinary morning he makes something close to six hundred decisions. On a bad morning he makes the first one at six forty, and everything else that day is a consequence of it.

Almost every sentence he says out loud has the same shape. If the ceiling stays below four hundred feet, they will hold the first departure. If they hold it, they will have to reroute two connections through Denver. Unless the crew signs on by half past seven, they will call the eight o’clock off entirely, and if that happens there will be a knock-on effect in three cities before lunch. He says the shape is not a habit. It is the job. “Nobody in here is predicting anything,” he says. “We are just being honest about what is attached to what.”

The part he says people misunderstand is the waiting. There is always a window — a stretch of forty or fifty minutes in which a decision is still possible — and the temptation is to spend it looking for certainty. He has learned not to. “If I wait until I am sure, the window has closed and the weather has decided for me. And the weather is not accountable to anyone.” So he decides early, and he keeps a backup plan for the decision he has just made, which he describes as the only genuinely useful thing anybody taught him in nine years.

One move gets used more than any other, and it is not a solution. Announcing a one-hour delay fixes nothing at all: the aircraft is still where it was, the crew is still in traffic. What it does is buy time. It converts a decision he cannot make yet into a decision he will be able to make at half past seven, with two crews on standby and a schedule that is tight but not yet impossible. He is careful about how often he uses it. “Buy time twice and you have bought yourself an afternoon. Buy it four times and you have just moved the whole problem into the evening, and now it is somebody else’s.”

The sheet he writes on has a column most people would not expect. Next to every condition there is a time: decide by 06:45, decide by 07:10, notify by 07:40. He says the column is the entire discipline of the room, and that he has seen more damage done by conditions with no deadline than by wrong decisions. “Everybody can tell you what might go wrong. Almost nobody tells you when they have to know. A condition with no time on it is not a decision. It is a worry, and worries do not go ahead or get called off. They just sit there getting bigger.”

listenings.text: The hardest decision of my day happens at about six forty in the morning, before most of the building is awake. It is whether to hold the first departure. And the thing people outside this room never believe is that I do not have the information yet. I will not have it for another half an hour. If I wait until I am certain, the window has closed and the weather has made the decision for me, and the weather is not accountable to anybody. So I decide early, on incomplete information, and then I keep a backup plan for the decision I have just made. The other thing I want to say is about delays. Announcing a one hour delay does not fix anything. The aircraft is still where it was. The crew is still in traffic. What it does is buy time, and buying time is very often the only move available to me. But be careful with it. Buy time twice and you have bought yourself an afternoon. Buy it four times and you have moved the whole problem into the evening, and now it belongs to somebody else.

There is an experiment from the nineteen nineties that has been repeated so many times it is almost boring, and the result never moves. Researchers asked final year students to predict when they would finish their thesis. Not the optimistic date. The realistic one. On average they said thirty four days. The real average was fifty six, and fewer than half of them were finished by the day they had been confident about. Now here is the part that makes it interesting rather than depressing. When the same students were asked to predict how long a friend would take, they were remarkably accurate. The optimism only appears when the plan belongs to you. It is not laziness and it is not vanity. It is that when you imagine your own project you imagine the path where nothing goes wrong, because that is the only path you can picture in detail. Everybody else's delays are visible to you. Your own are hypothetical. The fix that actually works is almost insultingly simple. Stop asking how long this will take, and start asking how long the last five things like it actually took.
